text: I’ll model the 8 mm cell width as the **clear opening across flats**, with 1 mm solid web between neighboring openings (9 mm flat-normal pitch). I’ll center a pointy-hex lattice on the 80 mm square and keep only complete cells, leaving at least a 1 mm perimeter frame. The flow axis is \(z\): 40 mm upstream, 20 mm core, and 80 mm downstream. I’ll first lay out and inspect this coarsest exact lattice before performing the 3D boolean and meshing.

The coarse layout is centered and leaves a continuous perimeter band; it contains 67 full cells. Next I’ll construct the solid plate and subtract the 67 through-prisms, then form the air volume as the complete duct minus that plate. I’ll measure volume and bounding extents before exporting anything.

The installed API confirms direct algebra-mode primitives and extrusion. I’ll now make the exact B-rep in metres; the cell openings are generated from the already inspected vertices and cut through the 20 mm plate in one boolean operation.

The B-rep is one connected fluid solid, has the requested 80 × 80 × 140 mm extent, and its volume matches the independent prism-area calculation to numerical precision. I’ll tessellate and render this exact fluid boundary now, looking both along the flow and obliquely to verify the through-cells and the upstream/downstream plenums.

I’ll save the exact fluid as a unitless OpenCASCADE BREP whose numerical coordinates are already metres, avoiding any STEP unit reinterpretation during meshing. The STL here is only for visual inspection.

The render confirms a continuous upstream plenum, 67 through-openings, and a longer downstream plenum. I’ll now assign boundary faces from their defining planes: \(z=0\) inlet, \(z=140\) mm outlet, the four original square-duct side planes as duct walls, and every remaining boundary face (core front/back lands plus cell sidewalls) as honeycomb walls. This avoids classifying curved or angled faces by bounding-box position.

All 414 boundary faces are assigned exactly once, with inlet and outlet areas each 6400 mm². I’ll import the metre-coordinate BREP into Gmsh and verify that its surface topology and the same defining-plane classification survive translation before generating tetrahedra.

The BREP translation preserves one volume, all 414 surfaces, and every patch area exactly. I’ll now generate the coarse tetrahedral mesh, using 2.8 mm in the plenums and 1.4 mm on honeycomb-boundary points so the 1 mm lands and hex corners are represented without immediately creating a production-scale mesh. Physical names are embedded for `gmshToFoam`.

The coarse mesh generated successfully. It is relatively dense (about 149k nodes) because every 1 mm land and 402 internal wall faces constrain the tetrahedra. I’ll convert it to OpenFOAM and inspect the conversion log and patch table before quality checking.

Conversion produced 779,380 tetrahedra and exactly the four requested named patches. The “undefined faces” conversion warning is Gmsh’s normal pre-mapping count; its 92,876 faces equal the final four patch face counts exactly, and no `defaultFaces` patch remains. I’ll now run the binding OpenFOAM quality check.

The mesh itself was not read: the optional `-allTopology` mode requests an `fvSchemes` dictionary that a geometry-only case does not otherwise need. I’ll run standard `checkMesh`, which performs the binding topology and geometry checks without introducing solver dictionaries or boundary conditions.

This OpenFOAM build requires the standard empty numerical dictionaries even for plain `checkMesh`. I’ll add only minimal `fvSchemes` and `fvSolution` headers—no fields, solver setup, or boundary conditions—then rerun the check.

`checkMesh` now passes: one connected region, closed combined boundary, 779,380 tetrahedra, maximum aspect ratio 7.23, maximum non-orthogonality 67.79°, maximum skewness 0.932, and exact total volume 0.00084227 m³. I’ll make a final mesh rendering with an exterior view and a longitudinal cut to visually confirm the internal passages are actually meshed.

The OpenFOAM-to-VTK export also finds all four patches. I’ll render those patches by name and overlay a center-plane slice of the volume mesh; this is the final visual inspection rather than another geometry operation.

The final image confirms the four patch identities and shows the center-plane tetrahedra passing through the honeycomb channels between the two plenums. I’ll remove only temporary visualization/conversion files and record the requested dimensions, measured results, mesh statistics, and the one lattice-edge assumption in the case.
